title: The rain on the plants (Kern ch. 5)
hookLine: one rain falls on all plants, and each grows by its own nature

lines: A STORM WITH NO GARDEN PLAN.
cards: A summer storm doesn't check the garden plan before it rains. The same water lands on the tomatoes, the weeds by the fence, the old maple and the moss between the paving stones.
And the next morning each has done something different with it. The tomato swells. The maple pushes out new leaves.
The moss turns bright green. In chapter five of the Lotus, the Buddha answers the disciples' story, and he chooses weather.

teach.h: A CLOUD OVER THE WHOLE WORLD.
teach.b: In Kern's translation the Buddha tells Kasyapa of a great cloud that rises and spreads over the whole world, covering everything.
Then it rains, everywhere at once, on grasses, bushes, herbs and trees, small, middle-sized and large, on every growing thing on mountains, in valleys and on the plains. The rain doesn't choose.
It is one rain, the sutra says, of a single taste.

teach.h: ONE RAIN, EACH PLANT ITS OWN WAY.
teach.b: But each plant takes up the water by its own nature and size, and grows, flowers and bears fruit in its own way. A blade of grass doesn't become an oak. It becomes more fully grass.
The Buddha says he is like that cloud.
He appears in the world and teaches gods, humans and all beings alike, and his teaching has one taste: the taste of release. He doesn't hold some back and pour more on others.
He is equal toward everyone, the noble and the poor, those who keep the rules and those who break them, the quick and the slow. The difference is in the receiving.
Each hears the teaching by their own capacity, and grows from there. This fits the last few days. In chapter two the teaching took many shapes.
Here the source of all those shapes is one.
The many ways belong to the hearers, like the many plants.

The one goal belongs to the rain. It doesn't ask the grass to be a tree, or the tree to apologize for being tall. It just keeps raining on everyone, and lets each grow toward the same light in the way only it can.

how: The parable of the medicinal plants in chapter five of the Lotus Sutra is taught in East Asian Buddhism as a picture of the Buddha's equal compassion: one teaching, received differently by each person according to their capacity.

games.q: what does “the rain on the plants” mean?
o: an old sign that a good harvest is coming to the village
a blessing that falls only on the people who earn it
one teaching of one taste, received by each in its own way

games.q: one rain, many plants: tap the pairs.
p: the Buddha appearing in the world
the teaching, of a single taste
beings, each by their own nature

s: in the parable the rain falls more heavily on the biggest trees
it is one rain, falling everywhere alike; the difference is in what each plant takes up.
the Buddha says he is equal toward those who keep the rules and those who break them
chapter five says his teaching goes to all alike, the noble and the poor, the quick and the slow.
the parable says every plant must grow into the same kind of tree
each grows, flowers and fruits according to its own nature.

games.q: you are a small herb under a great tree when the rain comes. what happens to you?
o: the tree takes all the water first
you take up what you can and grow as an herb
you grow into a tree yourself
games.why: the rain falls on all alike, and each plant takes it up by its own nature and size; the herb grows fully as an herb.

practice: If there's a plant near you, give it some water now, slowly, and watch the soil take it in; if not, picture one. Then breathe, each in-breath arriving like rain and each out-breath the plant quietly using it.
No hurry; let it take what it can.

wordCard.voice: The rain on the plants. The Buddha's parable in chapter five: one rain of one taste falls on every plant, and each grows by its own nature. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: medicinal plants, herbs; the name of chapter five in Kern's Sanskrit text.
